questions.q: Why does this retail inventory platform need two different freshness targets?
options: The restock trigger needs on-hand counts under 5 minutes stale, while nightly merchandising reports can tolerate a full day of staleness
Both consumers require exactly the same freshness target
Freshness targets are irrelevant to retail inventory systems
Merchandising reports require fresher data than the restock trigger
questions.explain: Two consumers with genuinely different needs is why one SLA can't serve both.

questions.q: Why does Lambda architecture, rather than Kappa, actually fit this platform?
options: The restock trigger's running total and the nightly reconciliation against shipments/returns/shrinkage are genuinely different computations, not the same logic replayed
Lambda is always the correct choice regardless of the computations involved
This platform has no need for either Lambda or Kappa architecture
Kappa architecture is incapable of handling any retail data
questions.explain: Lambda earns its keep specifically when the speed and batch layers need materially different logic, which is true here.

questions.q: Why does this platform use shared tenancy rather than siloed tenancy?
options: Corporate merchandising needs to roll up inventory across every store and region in one query, which the siloed model actively works against
Siloed tenancy is always cheaper than shared tenancy
This platform has no multi-tenancy considerations at all
Shared tenancy is required by law for all retail systems
questions.explain: Cross-store rollups are a use case that requires the shared model, unlike the compliance-driven examples that force siloing.

questions.q: What actually differs between the restock trigger and the merchandising report, given they share one fact table?
options: Which materialized view of FactInventoryMovement each consumer reads — not the underlying schema itself
Each consumer requires a completely separate schema and grain
The fact table's grain changes depending on which consumer is reading it
There is no difference between what each consumer reads
questions.explain: One schema, one grain (per SKU per store per movement) — but a near-real-time rollup versus a nightly reconciled view.

questions.q: How does this case study serve as a counter-example to Lesson 20's ride-sharing platform?
options: It shows that not every platform reduces to one replayable Kappa codepath — sometimes two genuinely different computations justify Lambda's extra cost
It shows that Kappa architecture is always the wrong choice
It shows that retail platforms never need real-time processing
It shows that ride-sharing platforms should also use Lambda architecture
questions.explain: Lesson 20 used one Kappa pipeline because one logic served both needs; this platform's two computations genuinely differ.
